Ao contrátrio do que dizem os espaços mais vazios fazem parte da ambientação do jogo. História boa, mesmo sendo simples e é sobre isso, parte do mistérios é fazer o jogador imaginar possibilidades. Fazia muito tempo que não me divertia tanto com um jogo. A exploração é muito recompensadora e exige atenção para encontrar locais com itens. No geral recomento a todos que querem se divertir com uma história simples e profunda se o jogador se permitir mergulhar nessa lua cheia de mistério. Parabéns aos desenvolvedores!!

What a trainwreck of a game [b]Ghost Song[/b] turned out to be.
A trainwreck that after a drizzle and a few years was overgrown by moss and you’ll take pictures because it’s so moody and serene and you’ll find yourself thinking about it from time to time.
But a trainwreck nonetheless. 

[h1]X-Factor[/h1]
The ambience is phenomenal, easily the best part, and hook, of the game.
The minimal score with long droning sounds made with strange instruments, and sprawling colorful alien planet battered with mist and humidity is a total mood.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
HEAVILY inspired by the genre moniker Metroid, explore an interconnected 2D map where places are locked behind weapons or movement options requiring them to unlock or reach those places so you’ll have to run through and revisit parts of the map with new and improved powers the next time around.

[h1]Story[/h1]
You the control of an amnesiac robot awakening on a planet overgrown with vegetation, armed (heh) with an arm cannon you’ll start to explore this weird world.

The story is solely told through character interaction where they’ll dump on you a lot of dialogue before resuming your exploring.

[h1]Downsides[/h1]
The game single most glaring flaw that completely breaks it in two if the feeling that the devs had the mindset of “put some stuff in the game first, figure out how it should work later” but never got to the second part due to someone suddenly yelling TIME OUT!
The result is this broken, unbalanced, underdeveloped mess where you see a lot of elements where an incredible amount of work and thought has been put into, meshed with others that feel they have been stitched together in 10 minutes.

The paper doll animation on display looks somewhat good only on the main character and some enemies while everything else looks like a cardboard cutout with pins on their joints.

Story may be a good blend of personal and succinct, but the characters themselves are so boring that the effort is completely invalidated.

I really, really liked this game, but for some reasons that feel difficult to explain and other reasons that I should not be giving full explanation at risk of spoiling the story. The soundtrack at first seemed peculiar and at odds with the setting of the game, but over time I began to notice how poignant and austere it was through careful drawn-out pauses and slow melodies that never really feel like they're bound to conclude with any comforting resolution. This sense was sustained throughout the rest of this game's story. While you are meant to battle some of the things that attempt to harm you, you are also meant to bring into question what and who these beings are while piecing together an understanding of what is happening on and around that world. Additionally, each fact you uncover in this world threatens to shed some light on what and who you might be. This alone made for an incredible game--add onto that some great metroidvania-like gameplay mechanics, complex characters, and environments that offer both beauty and danger, and you have this amazing gem.

Ghost Song is the story of a good game buried beneath a lot of very bad design choices aimed at wasting your time and patience. It's a game I loved and hated in equal parts, and whether I would recommend it depends on how much you can live with its many flaws to get to the good parts.

People complain about runbacks in Silksong, but Ghost Song adds another mechanic where, after each death, you lose a (admittedly tiny) chunk of your healthbar and can only repair it at various robot statues that are pretty scarce in the entire game, and against whom a boss runback is nothing. There's no good reason for this design choice other than wasting your time and goodwill, and the game loves to do that.

Do you need those chunks of healthbar? Not initially, though, after a couple of losses to the same boss, they add up, and they create this nagging feeling that really starts to bother you the more often you get defeated. Add to this the usual terrible design choice copied from soulslop games to lose your experience/money upon death (you can get it back, but only if you don't die a second time before reaching it), and it feels like the game is deliberately designed to waste your time.

To this, the game adds spongy bosses, which, at least in one case (Old Singer), will really tax your patience since that boss repeatedly runs away if you don't attack him in close contact. The game generally tries to limit how you fight bosses. Once you're in a boss area, some barriers appear that make it impossible to leave and usually impossible to snipe from afar. Which wouldn't be a problem if you weren't limited by stamina (which the bosses don't seem to be), and they move faster.

The add insult to injury, the game has a level up mechanic where you can either increase gun, health, or resolve (which does a couple of things), but those level ups add so little that it feels almost not worth it. It definitely is, but like everything in the game its designed to make your progress feel slow and cumbersome. After I played a bit, I felt like I was twenty hours into the game, but in reality barely scratched eight, which shows just how much of the game feels like a slog.

Which is kinda a shame, because behind all those terrible design choices hides a game with a genuinely unique environment that manages to evoke an alien world better than many of its contemporary Metroid-likes. Add to this writing and NPCs that made me genuinely interested in their stories and what happened to them, the mystery behind the character I was playing, and the background of the world I was exploring.

Though even with that, there are issues. You meet characters either in a special camp or all over the place, and after certain situations, they change what they are saying, and if you haven't talked to them up to those moments, you're cut off from finishing their personal stories (and achievements if these things matter to you). This works if you have a game with a few locales, and where it is clear where the NPCs will likely turn up. 

Aside from the camp people, most NPC locations seem utterly random, and after every story gate, you either exhaustively go all over the map again in hopes of finding them or give up on following their storylines. If there was at least a certain logic to this, it wouldn't matter so much, but as it is, it really feels like it's down to pure luck whether you stumble over certain characters.

And like I said, I actually like the NPC stories here, whether it's their personal history or whether it ties into the larger story of what happened to the world you're on. There are also moments you only unlock if you do some rather convoluted stuff, and how you should find that out without looking at a guide, I have no idea. That's just a terrible way to design secrets.

Other points of contention are somewhat floaty controls, though once you get a couple of movement upgrades, you can mitigate that a bit. The initial hours of the game are a bit of a pain in the ass due to that. Also, the map is suboptimal, and the markers are mostly useless. And the game doesn't pause when you're looking at the map or in the item menu, another bad design choice copied from soulslop games.

For all my complaints, though, once you get into the game, learn how it operates and how it tries to annoy you, it genuinely becomes one of the better Metroid-like metroidvania I've played for some time. A world with a very interesting science fiction backstory that reminds me of elements of Stephen Baxter's Xeelee cycle, but offered in a way that feels all its own. I just wish all those qualities weren't buried so deep under terrible design choices that make it impossible to really recommend the game.

The game is inspired by Metroid, yet the devs have missed the most important lesson from their inspiration: Difficulty design. On the one side the fighting mechanics are sluggish and annoying, but that's not what kills the vibe. It's the developer not understanding that when you're giving the player a sluggish character, you're communicating: [i]You are not an agile fighter, so avoid close combat like a plague![/i]

And then they throw you into a group of enemies without escape, without preparation and with a clearly underdeveloped character. Basically like your father simply throwing you into the deep water so you learn to swim on your own. [b]That's not how Metroid would ever do it[/b] and as such this is just a horrible failure in game pace.

If i have to try a scene 10+ times in the first 2 hours (!!) then you simply lost me. And you should be ashamed. The fact that most other reviews are kinda like "And then i started on easy..." explains how many people failed there. That should have been caught in beta, yet 3 years after release that's what is in the game.

Which is a pity, because the graphics are great, i like the atmosphere and the sound - All done visibly by professionals. Sadly the game designer hasn't even learned the bloody beginning lessons.

I find Ghost Songs graphics and music really interesting, this and the hope of a more Metroid-like Metroidvania where you [b]shoot mainly[/b] made me grab it. But not only does the projectiles of most guns [b]get weaker the further they travel[/b] with a very limited range, the gun also [b]overheats which reduces the projectiles damage and range even further.[/b]

Ghost Song feels like a [b]game running after trends,[/b] as it feels like a bargain bin [i]Souls-Like[/i] in a Metroidvania dressup without anything that makes it special. So nothing makes it stands out from all the other [i]Souls-like Metroidvanias[/i] that one can buy, other then it's unique collection of mechanics and unique atmosphere.

It has a few of Dark Souls-like systems where you collect points which are then used to level up where you select one of 3 stats. You also have [i]Energy[/i] and [i]Stamina[/i] where [i]Energy[/i] is used for the Special Shots and [i]Stamina[/i] is used for Running and the Dodge-Dash. When you die all your points stay where you died and need to be picked up. You have something akin to the "Estus Flask" to heal.

In order to "equip" shots and other tools you have a point based maximum allowance system where at the start you have 4 points of "Power Use" and shots & tools use a certain amount of those points. Which do increase each level-up.

You can shoot with your base shot, a special shot and melee. The shots do less damage the further they travel and your weapon "overheats" at which point you do bonus melee damage which I guess is supposed to encourage to do melee. On a character with a Arm Cannon to melee looks to me like a clowns show.

It also regresses on [b]upgrades[/b] the Metroidvania genre got by [b]not having a mini-map[/b] so you are forced to open the menu everytime you want to know where you are and the displayed map is not even [i]anywhere near[/i] the actual map. 

Additionally there are [b] so many rooms that are totally empty of enemies[/b] and the enemies that are there... are mostly enemies with attack patterns that make them [b]annoying to fight[/b] and kill off any fun the game had.

Other reviews speak of spots with "difficulty spikes" which are usually a enemy with a HP pools that feels like a sponge while having a annoying attack pattern that you... thanks to the also spongy controls since you use a [i]analogue control stick[/i] to move around in a 2D game will have a harder then needed time to evade.

Another one of Ghost Songs quirks is that [i]new enemies[/i] will spawn in [i]old areas[/i] at certain points of the game, making you have to keep run around the world over and over because those new spawned enemies usually have stuff they drop.

But for me [b]the worst part[/b] of Ghost Song is its controls, which feel like running around knee-deep in mud. I can only assume that the analogue stick controls where not realized in a good way.
Games where you use a analogue stick to move around can [b]never[/b] be as snappy in controls as any old 8bit, 16 bit or 32 bit game from back in the day. And one of the [b]main[/b] things important in a game is how you control it. Fail at that and the game is suddenly only 50% as fun as it could be. 

I also still don't really understand why [i]2D games[/i] feel the need to use an [i]analogue control stick[/i] for the movement when you never want to move your character at times [i]slower[/i] and at other times [i]faster,[/i] nor really have the need like in 3D 3rd person games to have more then 8 directions.

Additionally in Ghost Song when running around you can only aim in 8 directions while using a analogue controller, so unlike [i]Metroid Dread[/i] where you can aim in 360 degree there is no real need for an forced [i]analogue control stick[/i] ... and that "Aim Mode" where the game allows 360 degree of aiming while the character stands still is trash, it doesn't really work well on my Xbox controller.
I don't think that the author thought it through well enough how the game would control with a [i]analogue control stick.[/i] I tried many games... in many cases 360 aiming doesn't work as well as those Developer think it does, since it is rather hard to really aim with a analovue stick having 360 degree of aiming.
But maybe I am just to old a ancient artifact that is stuck in its ways and would like the option to switch the controls to whatever it is [b]I feel comfortable with.[/b]

And of course that is disabled. Unless you do that outside of the game using Steams controller setup, what a shame. I thought we are finally in an age where players can setup how they want to play a game, seems even 30 years later game Devs still like to enforce their control scheme on players.

I really wanted to like Ghost Song, but in the end, I was left disappointed by wasted potential.

[b]The Good[/b]
* Level art is interesting and atmospheric.
* The music has its good moments.
* Voice-acted lines are well-delivered.

[b]The Bad[/b]
* The game loves to waste your time. Movement is slow, even the "fast" run feels sluggish. You can't move while aiming. Most melee weapons are slow. Energy reload is slow. The only elevator in the game locks you in a box that crawls upward. Voiced dialogue can't be skipped.

* You have to constantly manage three separate bars: gun overheating (shared with the special gun, which causes even faster overheating of basic shots), energy for the special gun, and stamina for melee, dashing, and running. I think the idea was to make you switch between melee and ranged attacks, but during boss fights I often could only just stand waiting for something to recharge.

* Boss fights don’t feel satisfying. Bosses charge to attack, then stand in place. You're supposed to use melee during these openings, but you often don't have enough stamina left after dodging. The optimal (but boring) strategy ends up being: unload all alternate blaster shots, dodge, swing melee once or twice, trigger faster energy regen with a suit module after healing, repeat.

* Leveling is basically useless. Upgrades give tiny benefits for exponentially increasing costs. On my first playthrough, I went all-in on Resolve, hoping it would help with energy regen. It just made waiting for a bigger bar to refill take even longer. I thought I’d messed up, restarted and focused on Gun Power instead - only to find that it didn’t matter much either. The damage boost wasn’t significant.

* The module system feels heavily restricted. You're limited by suit power, and after equipping a few essential modules (primary stat scalers, NanoGel yield booster, alternate blaster), there's barely any power left for anything else. Most of the modules I found felt either too situational or just underwhelming, especially the gun mods, which were weaker (power and/or range) than the rocket you get early in the game.

* Exploration and backtracking are forced and unrewarding. You're sent across the map to collect scattered ship parts, but because of slow traversal, weak rewards, and underwhelming progression systems, the process just feels like padding.

* Level design lacks consistency. Some vertical shafts are traversable, others are just decoration. Some alternate paths lead nowhere. Some breakable walls are one-way, some two-way, and only a few are marked as such. Some tunnels appear on the map, one doesn't. Some rooms show detailed layout on the map, most don't. There are even passages shown in the wrong spot on the map. I wasted a lot of time trying to find secrets that turned out to be bad mapping.

* The story tries to explore deeper themes - purpose, sacrifice, spirituality, sense of self - but doesn't say anything meaningful. Characters (especially the ship crew) feel like mouthpieces for specific ideas rather than real people who are part of a coherent world. The narrative as a whole just doesn't make much sense. I got the point of the second ending, but how that fit murderer robot is beyond me.

[b]Final thoughts[/b]
It's not a terrible game, just not a very good one. I kept hoping there’d be something more to it by the end, but I finished feeling disappointed.
It's a beautiful shell, but with a bunch of sand instead of a pearl inside.
